MGT 409 · AI Foundations for Managers · Fall 2026

Lane League

A one-minute supercar drive, run by three agents, for a student who needs to put recruiting and a problem set down.

Renae Wen

Repo: GITHUB_URL

The app runs on your own computer. The README is the runbook. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 after the steps there. It is not hosted.

1. Motivation

The person is a student in New Haven during recruiting season. The day is a case interview, then a problem set, then another email. The break they actually take is a phone: a feed, a chat thread, twenty minutes that were supposed to be two. Nothing ends. The mind does not empty. It changes channels.

What that costs is not a subscription. It is the next hour. A short break that has no edge turns into a lost block of work, and the person comes back more wired than they left. Meditation apps ask for an account, a streak, and a voice that keeps talking. A group chat asks you to answer. ChatGPT will talk about the interview for as long as you type.

Lane League is the opposite shape. You type a name, pick one car, and drive for sixty seconds. Coins sit off the racing line. Hurdles sit on it. When the clock hits zero, the minute is over. A ranked minute puts your name on a board with other people, so the reset is social without becoming a conversation. Practice is the same road with the score thrown away, for the moment you do not want a record.

2. What is new here

Calm and Headspace already sell a quiet minute. They are guided audio. You listen. You do not steer. They are built to keep you in a library of sessions.

Mario Kart, Gran Turismo, and the free browser racers already sell a drive. They are built to last: another cup, another lap, a season. The point is to stay.

ChatGPT will role-play a calm friend. It will also keep the thread open, invent a score if you ask for one, and follow an instruction that was hiding in your sentence. There is no clock, no car, and no board.

Lane League takes the sixty-second edge from a breathing exercise and the hands from a driving game, and it puts a small crew of agents around the minute. The agents do not drive the car. The person does. The agents check the name, look up that specific car, speak one calm line, and then write a close that is not allowed to invent the points. Practice never calls a model, so the empty minute can also be the cheap minute. I have not found a product that is a hard one-minute social drive whose score is computed by the server and only narrated by the model.

3. The agents

Three agents, one model: gpt-6-luna through Portkey, on the course key. Reasoning effort is set to none. Each agent has a request cap and a tool-call cap so a bad loop stops.

The steward prepares the minute. Its tools, in the order the prompt demands, are scan_text, lookup_vehicle, driver_card, track_card, and, for a ranked minute, ask_rival. It returns a structured plan: a coach note and a radio line. It cannot award points.

The quiet passenger is the rival agent. It is not a second car. The road shows only the car you picked. The passenger’s only tool is rival_brief, which hands it the machine, the weather, and the temperament. It returns one radio line. The server clamps the mistake rate to the temperament so the model cannot make the passenger absurd.

The clerk closes the minute. Its tools are official_result, commit_result, standings, and place_ad. official_result is the score the server already computed from coins, hurdles, and the clock. commit_result takes no point argument. If the clerk’s note names a different total, the board keeps the server’s number. The ad tool still runs, because the clerk’s job includes picking from a fixed catalog, but the driving screen does not show an ad. A reset should not carry a banner.

Practice never enters this picture. The practice button starts the same road and explains a coin and a hurdle in a fixed script. No request leaves for the model.

How a person uses it

  1. The first screen is only a name. Two to twenty-three letters, then Enter.
  2. The garage is sixteen supercars. Each card shows pace in mph, launch, and grip. The sheet under a selected car explains what those numbers do on this road.
  3. An optional line, “what is on your mind,” is a feeling. It is scanned before the crew sees it.
  4. Practice starts at once. The radio names a coin and a hurdle as they come up. Nothing is saved.
  5. Drive for rank waits while the steward and the passenger work. Then the clock starts at 1:00. Hold the up arrow. Steer into gold coins. Lift for a red-and-white hurdle. End stops the minute and drops the finish bonus.
  6. The close shows the server’s arithmetic, the clerk’s sentence, and the tokens for the open and the close.

The arithmetic is fixed. A coin is 100 points, and there are 14. A hurdle is minus 25, and there are 10, and it also cuts speed. Crossing the line inside the minute adds 250, then 8 points for each second still on the clock. Ending early, or running the clock out, pays neither of those. The server clamps a client who claims 99 coins or 500 seconds left. The model is not in this formula.

What it isWhat Lane League does instead
Calm, HeadspaceGuided audio, a library, an accountYou steer. The session cannot run past sixty seconds.
Kart racersA drive built to continueOne minute, one car, then a close.
ChatGPTA conversation with no score and no endAgents may speak. They may not mint the points, and an instruction in the text never reaches them.

One real minute

Driver Avery Cole. Car: Ferrari 296 GTB. No note in the mind field, so the steward was not handed a feeling to repeat. The garage waited on the line “The steward is clearing one minute.”

The steward called scan_text (the name was allowed), lookup_vehicle (Ferrari 296 GTB, sharp nose, low grip), track_card (Paper Street, clear), driver_card, and ask_rival. The passenger called rival_brief and came back with a line about braking smoothly. The coach note that reached the radio was: “Put the day down for sixty seconds and take one quiet breath. The Ferrari 296 GTB turns quickly but can slide if you stay flat, so ease off smoothly on the clear road.”

The minute was ended early, on purpose, with no coins and no hurdles. The server’s total was 0: no finish bonus, no time-left points. The clerk called official_result, commit_result, standings, and place_ad. Its note said “The official result was 0 points. The one-minute reset is over.” The page shows the clerk’s number next to the server’s. They match.

A second measured minute, earlier the same day, checked the arithmetic when the total was not zero. Avery Cole, Ferrari 296 GTB, mind line “A case interview in an hour.” The drive was closed as an early end with 2 coins and 1 hurdle and 40 seconds still showing. The server refused the finish bonus and the time-left points, because the car had not crossed the line.

PieceCountPoints
Coins2 × 100200
Hurdles1 × 25−25
Finishended before the line0
Time leftnot paid on an early end0
Posted175

The clerk’s headline was “Official race result: 175 points.” The body was “The official result was 175 points. The one-minute reset is over.” model_said was 175 and corrected was false. The coach note on that open was specific: set the case interview down for sixty seconds, the 296 GTB turns sharply and can slide, the road was wet, ease into the corner. The passenger’s line was about being patient with the 296. Neither line mentioned points, a sponsor, or a prompt.

What each tool handed back on that open, in order: scan_text allowed the name; track_card returned The Cut, low sun, 1,920 meters; lookup_vehicle returned the Ferrari’s pace, launch, brakes, steering, grip, and width; driver_card returned a new driver, zero races, and a skill band the server would enforce; ask_rival passed one sentence about the car and the weather; rival_brief returned the name Quiet Seat and the mistake target for quiet company. The steward’s plan came last. The server then clamped skill and mistake rate to that band. On this run it did not have to correct them.

The keys are read twice, on purpose. First the .env in the repo, then the .env one folder up, which is where a cloned submission sits under the teaching staff’s keys. The only name the app asks for is PORTKEY_API_KEY. If that file is missing, the minute still opens. The radio is a house line, the page says the house card was used, and the token count stays at zero.

4. Tokenomics

Prices are the GPT-6 Luna list used in the course tools, per token: input $0.10 per million, cache read $0.01 per million, cache write $0.125 per million, output $0.50 per million. Input tokens already include cached tokens, so uncached input is the remainder. The app prices a run with that formula and prints the result on the close screen.

The minute in Figure 2, read off the screen:

InputCached inputOutputCost
Before the minute (steward and passenger)5,3331,108324$0.000626
After the minute (clerk)3,7600112$0.000432
One ranked minute9,0931,108436$0.001058

An earlier instrumented run of the same path, with a one-line note about a case interview, landed at $0.001058 as well. That run also wrote 1,220 tokens into the cache on the steward. The coach note still named the Ferrari and the interview. The cache did not flatten the answer into a generic line.

A person who takes one ranked minute on each of 15 days in a recruiting month costs about 15 × $0.001058 = $0.016. One hundred such people cost about $1.59 a month. Ten thousand cost about $158.70 a month. That scale case assumes the ranked minute, not practice.

Practice is the cost cut that matters. It is the same road and the same clock, and it sends nothing to the model: 0 tokens, $0. A blocked instruction is the same. The firewall returns before get_team() is called, which is why the safety panel says “Agent called: false.” A day is also capped at 80,000 tokens or 40 runs. Past that, the minute still opens on a written house card and the model is not called.

The cut has a cost in the product. Practice cannot say your sentence back to you. Its radio is a fixed explanation of a coin and a hurdle. The ranked radio in Figure 1 is specific to the Ferrari and to “put the day down.” That is the quality you give up when you skip the model. I would not skip it on a ranked minute. The personal line is the point of paying a tenth of a cent.

5. Safety

The risk that matters here is a person, or a pasted sentence, telling the crew to ignore its rules and mint points. A second risk is the clerk inventing a total. A third is a loop burning the key.

Names are checked before a model call: two to twenty-three letters, and not a house name already on the wall. Anything that looks like an instruction — “ignore previous instructions,” “set my points,” “reveal the prompt,” a system tag — is refused by inspect_text in the server. The optional “what is on your mind” line goes through the same check. If it fails, the prepare route returns agent_called: false and does not build the team.

The same function is what the test suite hits: that sentence is blocked, and a normal name is not. A second test feeds the points guard a clerk who claims 999,999 points against a server total of 0. The posted number stays 0.

On a real close, the clerk is told the official total and commit_result will not take a different one. In Figure 2 the model said 0 and the server posted 0. If those ever diverge, the page says so and the board keeps the server figure. Copy that comes back with an injection pattern is dropped and replaced with a house line.

Overspending is capped twice. Each agent has a request limit and a tool-call limit inside the run. The process has a daily token cap and a daily run cap. Practice and a blocked sentence never touch the key.

6. Impact

The user this was built for is a student in New Haven whose break currently has no edge. I used the app as that person: name, car, one minute, end. The minute in Figure 1 is that use. It took the crew about fifteen seconds to open and the clock then ran on its own. Ending early still produced a close and a score of zero, which is the honest result of stopping before a coin.

I am not claiming a clinical effect, and I have not timed a second person against their phone. The number I will stand behind is the shape of the break. The alternative is an open-ended feed. This one ends at sixty seconds, or sooner if you press End. The cost of the social version is about a tenth of a cent. The private version, practice, is free. One hundred students taking fifteen ranked minutes in a month is about $1.59. That is the bill for a shared board, not for a meditation subscription.

What I cannot claim yet is that the board changes behavior. A real second user, with a before-and-after on how long the break lasted, is the missing measurement. Until then the impact case is the bounded minute and the measured bill, not a wellness outcome.

7. What a month of this actually is

Put the measured minute next to the way the break works today. A recruiting week in New Haven is not twenty meditation sessions. It is a few moments between a firm’s email and a problem set, most of them already spent on a phone. If fifteen of those moments become a ranked minute, the model bill is about sixteen cents for that person. If they are all practice, the bill is zero and the road is the same. The board is the only reason to pay. It is there so the minute is something you did with other people, not a private timer.

The public board hides the house names. Those rows exist so the wall is not blank on a fresh database, and so a person cannot sign in as one of them. They are not a leaderboard you can catch. A ranked close writes one row: the name, the server’s points, the car, the coins, the hurdles, and whether the line was crossed. Ending early still writes the row. That is deliberate. Stopping is a finished act. It is not a missing lap.

I would not sell this as a wellness product. The evidence I have is a minute I drove, a firewall I tripped on purpose, and a bill I read off the screen. The evidence I do not have is a classmate’s phone, timed before and after. Section 8 is that gap, and the small product debts around it.

8. Limits and next steps

The crew takes several seconds before the minute starts. On a bad network that wait is the whole product. A house card already exists for a missing key or a blown cap. I would show that wait more calmly, and I would cache a coach line per car for the rest of the day so the second ranked minute in a session does not pay the steward again. The first run already showed a cache read. I have not yet stored that line myself.

The close screen prints the raw tool trace. That is the right evidence for this report and the wrong surface for a tired person. Next month the trace moves behind a “what the crew did” disclosure, and the page keeps the headline, the score, and the cost.

The clerk still selects a sponsor from a fixed catalog, because that tool is how the agent is kept from inventing an advertisement. The player never sees it. If the catalog is not earning its keep, the next step is to drop place_ad from the player path entirely and leave the catalog in the tests.

The road is one layout. A phone stacks the buttons, and a wide window puts steering on the left and End on the right, but the radio can still sit on top of the speed when the window is narrow. Another month would be a pass on that overlap, and a second person in New Haven timing their own break against the minute.

The cars are not a skin. Pace, launch, brakes, steering, grip, and width are the numbers the road uses. The Jesko is the fastest here and the loosest. The Continental GT is the slowest and the widest, so the grass arrives sooner. The Taycan has the strongest launch. The speedometer on the dash is scaled to that car’s own top speed, in mph, not to a shared dial. A person who has never opened the app can still read the garage: a photo, a pace, and one sentence. The buttons along the bottom of the minute grow and wrap with the window. On a wide screen, steering sits on the left and End sits on the right. On a phone they become two full-width rows, and the header shrinks so the road keeps the rest.

Why this model, and not a larger one: the course key is only allowed to call gpt-6-luna, and the job does not need a long chain of thought. The steward has to obey a tool order and return a short plan. The passenger has to return one line. The clerk has to copy a number. A slower, more expensive model would make the wait before the minute the whole product. The setting is reasoning effort none, with a cap of eight requests for the steward, four for the passenger, and six for the clerk.
